title: Chapter 2.  History — Migration & the Colonial Period

blocks.content: Mizo history before British contact is understood primarily through oral tradition and clan migration accounts rather than written chronicles - this chapter traces the Mizo people's traditional migration narrative and the subsequent British 'Lushai Hills' annexation.

Mizo oral tradition traces the community's origins to a legendary point of ancestral emergence traditionally called 'Chhinlung' (sometimes described as a cave or a large rock from which the ancestors of the Mizo and related peoples are said to have emerged), followed by a long, multi-generational southward and westward migration - via what is now Myanmar and China's Yunnan/Chin Hills border region - before eventually settling the hill tracts of present-day Mizoram, generally understood by historians to have taken place over recent centuries.

The Mizo (a collective term encompassing numerous related clans, historically also referred to by the British as 'Lushai', now considered a somewhat narrower or externally-imposed term for a subset of the wider Mizo community) share close ethnic, linguistic and cultural ties with related Chin and Kuki-Zo communities of neighbouring Myanmar, Manipur (Chapter 7 of the companion Manipur GS volume) and Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts, reflecting this shared migratory heritage across what is now an international and inter-state boundary.

★ EXAM POINT: 'Chhinlung' is the legendary point of ancestral origin in Mizo oral tradition - a frequently tested culture-history fact, alongside the broader recognition that the Mizo share close ethnic ties with the Chin (Myanmar) and Kuki-Zo (Manipur, Chapter 7 of the companion Manipur volume) communities.

British colonial contact with the Mizo Hills (then called the 'Lushai Hills' by the British) intensified through the late 19th century, driven partly by a series of raids and counter-raids between hill communities and British-administered tea-plantation areas of neighbouring Cachar (Assam), including the notable 1871-72 'Lushai Expedition' launched by the British in response to such raids.

The Lushai Hills were formally annexed and brought under direct British administration in 1890 (with the northern and southern portions of the hills initially administered somewhat separately before unification), subsequently incorporated into British India's Assam province as the 'Lushai Hills District' - a designation that persisted, with the later addition of 'Mizo' terminology, through the rest of the colonial period.

As in Meghalaya's Khasi/Jaintia/Garo Hills (covered in the companion Meghalaya GS volume) and Nagaland's Naga Hills, the British administered the Lushai Hills under a distinct, relatively 'light-touch' 'Excluded Area'/'Backward Tract' administrative framework, deliberately maintaining separation from the more directly governed plains districts - an administrative pattern that would later influence the post-Independence Sixth Schedule and special-provision frameworks (Chapter 5).

items: Mizo oral tradition traces ancestral origin to 'Chhinlung', followed by a long southward/westward migration via Myanmar/Yunnan border areas.
Mizo share close ethnic-linguistic ties with the Chin (Myanmar) and Kuki-Zo (Manipur) communities.
1871-72 Lushai Expedition; Lushai Hills formally annexed by the British in 1890, later organised as 'Lushai Hills District' of Assam.
British administered the Lushai Hills under a distinct 'Excluded Area'/'Backward Tract' framework, similar to other North-Eastern hill areas.
